task: This is a synthetic exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes as the fixed record: select, organize and phrase the story without inventing additional reported events, scenes, quotations or reporting activity. Write a headline and an explainer of roughly 450–650 words in AP style for general newspaper readers about gaps, suffixes and changed entrances in Westhollow's street-address system. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 18, 2026.

facts.text: The fictional Westhollow addressing office assigns identifiers to entrances and properties under a local numbering plan maintained separately from land-title records.
Most streets in the current plan use odd numbers on one side and even numbers on the other, so consecutive numbers need not be neighboring entrances.
Older streets retain some inherited numbering patterns that do not follow the current plan exactly.
The office has received questions after two former shop units were combined and a nearby property gained a new entrance.
In the office's fictional example, units formerly numbered 12 and 14 use 12 after combination, leaving 14 unused rather than renumbering the whole street.
A separate example uses 20A and 20B for two approved entrances where inserting ordinary whole numbers would conflict with existing addresses.
The examples explain the local system and are not the addresses of actual households supplied in this case.
Addressing officer Tessa Linn said, "A missing number may tell you about an old division of the street, not a missing building."
A new owner, shop name or business tenant does not automatically require a new street number.
The office assesses proposed address changes using entrance position, neighboring identifiers and the needs of services that locate the property.
An approved address change is communicated to relevant city services, but a business must still update its own signs, deliveries and customer information.
Shopkeeper Orin Fale said, "The city's record changed in one step. Our invoices, labels and delivery notes did not all change with it."
The city does not promise that every private map or delivery database will update at the same time.
The local process distinguishes a building's official street identifier from internal apartment or suite numbers.
An internal unit renumbering can still affect emergency and delivery information, so managers are asked to consult the addressing office before changing it.
The supplied process does not determine who owns a property or settle a dispute about a shared entrance.
The office preserves earlier address references so historical planning files can be connected to current locations.
Some older plans use the name of a former pub or workshop instead of a street number, requiring staff to compare several records.
The city is preparing a public explanation of the process after receiving repeated requests to fill apparent gaps simply for visual neatness.
The city has not proposed a townwide renumbering exercise.
No statistics about emergency-response delays or failed deliveries are included in the supplied office record.
The rules described are specific to Westhollow's records and should not be presented as identical practice in every town.

forbidden_additions: A missing number treated as proof of a missing building or a townwide renumbering plan.
Immediate updates to every private database.
A street identifier treated as proof of ownership or an invented emergency-delay statistic.
preserve: Entrances, property records and internal unit labels as related but different identifiers.
Historical continuity and the limits of the illustrative examples.
Exact quotation wording and attribution when quotations are used.
